desc:
You may cut the grid matrix along one straight line that runs between two neighbouring rows or between two neighbouring columns. A cut splits the grid into two non-empty parts. A cut is fair if the two parts have exactly the same sum.

Return the number of fair cuts. A horizontal cut and a vertical cut are different cuts, and different positions are different cuts.

matrix = [[1, 2],
          [2, 1]]
horizontal cut: 3 | 3  (fair)
vertical cut:   3 | 3  (fair)
result = 2
constraints: A grid with a single row has no horizontal cut; a grid with a single column has no vertical cut
hints: If the top part has sum s, what must the sum of the bottom part be for the cut to be fair?
A cut is fair exactly when the part on one side is half of the total sum. Compute the total first.
Compute the sum of every row and every column. A horizontal cut after row i is fair if the prefix sum of row sums equals total - prefix; do the same with column sums for vertical cuts.
editorial: Let total be the sum of all cells. A cut leaves a top part (or left part) with sum s and a remaining part with sum total - s, so the cut is fair if and only if 2 * s == total.

For horizontal cuts, walk through the rows keeping the running sum of row sums; every position between row i and row i + 1 (for i from 0 to R-2) is tested. Vertical cuts work the same on column sums. This is a one-dimensional prefix sum on the margins of the grid.
With negative values or zeros, several cuts of the same direction may all be fair, which is why the answer is a count. Time O(R * C), space O(R + C).
solution:
def countEqualCuts(matrix):
    R, C = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    rows = [sum(row) for row in matrix]
    cols = [sum(matrix[i][j] for i in range(R)) for j in range(C)]
    total = sum(rows)
    count = 0
    run = 0
    for i in range(R - 1):
        run += rows[i]
        if 2 * run == total:
            count += 1
    run = 0
    for j in range(C - 1):
        run += cols[j]
        if 2 * run == total:
            count += 1
    return count
